title: 1 Chronicles 11:10–25
context: The Chronicler introduces the chief of David’s mighty men, who helped make him king according to the LORD’s word. Jashobeam, Eleazar son of Dodo, and the deed in the barley field are named first. Three of the thirty break through the Philistine lines at Bethlehem to bring David water, which he pours out to the LORD rather than drink at the cost of their lives. Abishai, chief of the three, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who killed a lion and a tall Egyptian, are honored though neither attains to the three. The parallel is 2 Samuel 23:8–23. Several names and numbers differ, including three hundred in 1 Chronicles 11:11 against eight hundred in 2 Samuel 23:8, and the names Jashobeam and Josheb Basshebeth; Chronicles also has no separate account of Shammah. These differences are named rather than resolved.

verses.text: Now these are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who showed themselves strong with him in his kingdom, together with all Israel, to make him king, according to the LORD’s word concerning Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The Chronicler introduces the chief mighty men, who helped make David king according to the LORD’s word. Arminian readers note that the list honors real people whose faithful service mattered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God raising up helpers around His anointed king, in line with His word. Both traditions note that Chronicles places this list at the start of David’s reign, while 2 Samuel 23:8 places it near the end of David’s story.

verses.text: This is the number of the mighty men whom David had: Jashobeam, the son of a Hachmonite, the chief of the thirty; he lifted up his spear against three hundred and killed them at one time.
verses.arminianNotes: Jashobeam, chief of the thirty, kills three hundred at one time. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 23:8 names him Josheb Basshebeth and gives eight hundred; the differences are noted rather than resolved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God working through extraordinary courage. Shared ground: as the 2 Samuel 23 notes say, these name and number differences are textual issues, and both traditions read the verse as honoring faithful service.

verses.text: After him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite, who was one of the three mighty men.
verses.arminianNotes: Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite is one of the three mighty men. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 23:9 gives his father’s name as Dodai, a spelling difference noted in the 2 Samuel notes as well.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see loyalty to the LORD’s anointed in Eleazar’s place among the three. Both traditions read the verse as introducing a deed of courage, without building anything on the spelling differences.

verses.text: He was with David at Pasdammim, and there the Philistines were gathered together to battle, where there was a plot of ground full of barley; and the people fled from before the Philistines.
verses.arminianNotes: Eleazar is with David at Pasdammim, where the people flee from the Philistines in a barley field. Arminian readers note that Pasdammim’s location is uncertain, and the scene focuses on standing firm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Samuel 23:11 describes a similar stand by Shammah in a field of lentils. Shared ground: how the two accounts relate is a textual issue, noted in the 2 Samuel notes as well, and not resolved here.

verses.text: They stood in the middle of the plot, defended it, and killed the Philistines; and the LORD saved them by a great victory.
verses.arminianNotes: They stand in the plot, defend it, and kill the Philistines, and the LORD saves them by a great victory. Arminian readers note that human courage and God’s action are held together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the victory is credited to the LORD. Both traditions agree, as in the 2 Samuel 23 notes, that God works through human courage and that the glory belongs to Him.

verses.text: Three of the thirty chief men went down to the rock to David, into the cave of Adullam; and the army of the Philistines were encamped in the valley of Rephaim.
verses.arminianNotes: Three of the thirty go down to David at the rock, to the cave of Adullam, while the Philistines camp in the valley of Rephaim. Arminian readers note the setting in David’s fugitive years (compare 1 Samuel 22:1).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the loyalty of David’s men in a hard season. Shared ground: the verse parallels 2 Samuel 23:13, which mentions harvest time; the location of Adullam is generally placed in the lowland of Judah, though not certainly.

verses.text: David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was in Bethlehem at that time.
verses.arminianNotes: David is in the stronghold, and a Philistine garrison is in Bethlehem. Arminian readers note the irony that David’s hometown is under enemy control while he waits in hiding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the hardship of the anointed king not yet ruling his own land. Both traditions read the verse as parallel to 2 Samuel 23:14, and note that the identity of “the stronghold” here is uncertain.

verses.text: David longed, and said, “Oh, that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem, which is by the gate!”
verses.arminianNotes: David longs for water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate. Arminian readers note the very human longing for home, expressed as a wish rather than a command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an honest expression of homesickness that his men take as an occasion to show devotion. Shared ground: the verse parallels 2 Samuel 23:15, and both traditions read the longing simply, without symbolic meaning.

verses.text: The three broke through the army of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate, took it, and brought it to David; but David would not drink any of it, but poured it out to the LORD,
verses.arminianNotes: The three break through the Philistine army, draw water, and bring it, but David pours it out to the LORD. Arminian readers note David’s recognition that such a costly gift belongs to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the water poured out as an offering, too precious for personal use. Both traditions read the act as reverence and gratitude, as the 2 Samuel 23:16 notes do, and neither reads more into the water itself.

verses.text: and said, “My God forbid me, that I should do this! Shall I drink the blood of these men who have put their lives in jeopardy?” For they risked their lives to bring it. Therefore he would not drink it. The three mighty men did these things.
verses.arminianNotes: David says God forbid that he drink the blood of men who risked their lives. Arminian readers note that he values his men’s lives above his own desire; 2 Samuel 23:17 has “Be it far from me, LORD.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the image of blood as life given at great risk. Shared ground: the verse shows a leader who refuses to profit from others’ sacrifice, a lesson both traditions draw, without treating the water as a symbol.

verses.text: Abishai, the brother of Joab, was chief of the three; for he lifted up his spear against three hundred and killed them, and had a name among the three.
verses.arminianNotes: Abishai, Joab’s brother, is chief of the three and kills three hundred with his spear. Arminian readers note that Abishai’s courage is honored despite his sometimes rash character elsewhere (1 Samuel 26:8).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God can use a man of fierce temperament for good ends. The verse corresponds to 2 Samuel 23:18, where Abishai is also called the son of Zeruiah, and both traditions take it as straightforward praise of his valor.

verses.text: Of the three, he was more honorable than the two, and was made their captain; however he wasn’t included in the three.
verses.arminianNotes: Abishai is more honorable than the two and made their captain, yet he is not included in the three. Arminian readers note the puzzling ranking, which shows distinctions among David’s warriors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Samuel 23:19 phrases the comparison as “most honorable of the three”; the wording differs, and the exact sense of the ranking is discussed. Shared ground: Abishai holds high honor without belonging to the three.

verses.text: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done mighty deeds, killed the two sons of Ariel of Moab. He also went down and killed a lion in the middle of a pit on a snowy day.
verses.arminianNotes: Benaiah son of Jehoiada, of Kabzeel, kills the two sons of Ariel of Moab and a lion in a pit on a snowy day. Arminian readers note the vivid deeds that made him famous among David’s men.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Benaiah’s courage as preparing him for later service, including under Solomon (1 Kings 2:35). Both traditions read the verse as parallel to 2 Samuel 23:20, while the meaning of “Ariel” here is uncertain.

verses.text: He killed an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits high. In the Egyptian’s hand was a spear like a weaver’s beam; and he went down to him with a staff, plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and killed him with his own spear.
verses.arminianNotes: Benaiah kills an Egyptian five cubits tall, roughly seven and a half feet by common reckoning, with the man’s own spear. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 23:21 calls him huge but gives no height.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God enabling a smaller man to defeat a stronger enemy, recalling David and Goliath. Shared ground: the spear like a weaver’s beam echoes 1 Samuel 17:7, and both traditions read the verse as honoring courage.

verses.text: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada did these things and had a name among the three mighty men.
verses.arminianNotes: Benaiah does these things and has a name among the three mighty men. Arminian readers note that his reputation rests on real deeds of bravery and loyalty, recognized by his peers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that a reputation earned in battle later made Benaiah a trusted commander. The verse matches 2 Samuel 23:22 almost word for word and wraps up the record of his exploits before David appoints him.

verses.text: Behold, he was more honorable than the thirty, but he didn’t attain to the three; and David set him over his guard.
verses.arminianNotes: Benaiah is more honorable than the thirty but does not attain to the three, and David sets him over his guard. Arminian readers note that David entrusts his personal safety to a proven man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Benaiah’s appointment as part of God’s provision of faithful servants around David. Shared ground: the verse parallels 2 Samuel 23:23, and both traditions read it as honoring loyalty and trust.
